work: Enarratio in Epistolam B. Pauli ad Romanos
source: Dionysii Cartusiani Opera Omnia, t. XIII (Montreuil)

1.title: PROSECUTIO EXPOSITIONIS HUJUS PRIMI CAPITULI, AB EO LOCO QUO DICITUR : NON ENIM ERUBESCO EVANGELIUM.
1.title_en: Continuation of the exposition of this first chapter, from the place where it says: For I am not ashamed of the Gospel.

paras.t: Merito dixi me esse paratum evangelizare et vobis Romanis : Non enim erubesco Evangelium, hoc est, non confundor publice annuntiare crucem et passionem ac cetera mysteria Christi, quæ in Evangelio describuntur, atque a reprobis irridentur. Paratus sum namque pro nomine Jesu contumeliam pati, quoniam ipse ait : Qui me erubuerit et meos sermones, hunc Filius hominis erubescet, quum venerit in regno suo. Huic consonat illud Psalmistæ : Et loquebar in testimoniis tuis in conspectu regum, et non confundebar. Ratio hujus subjicitur : Virtus enim Dei est in salutem omni credenti, hoc est, Evangelium Christi est virtus, id est potens effectus divinæ potestatis, seu fortis doctrina, proficiens in salutem æternam omni credenti per fidem formatam ac perseverantem, Judæo primum, hoc est ex Judaismo conversis, videlicet primitivæ Ecclesiæ, quæ ex Judæis constabat. Nam et Christus dicebat : Non sum missus nisi ad oves quæ perierunt domus Israel, hoc est, ad Synagogam primo ac principaliter missus sum. Ideo Paulus aiebat Judæis : Vobis oportebat primum loqui verbum Dei. Deinde et Græco, hoc est ex gentilitate conversis, valet Evangelium. Per Græcos, quasi a digniori, gentiles significat. Repulsa enim prædicatione Apostolorum a Judæis, justa facta est transmigratio ad gentiles, secundum quod Paulus testatur : Quia repulistis illud, et indignos vos judicastis vitæ æternæ, ecce convertimur ad gentes. Secundum Haymonem, Evangelium dicitur virtus Dei, quoniam Christum Dei virtutem annuntiat. Secundum Ambrosium vero, dicitur virtus Dei, quoniam valet ad indulgentiam peccatorum, et ad operationem miraculorum.
paras.en: Rightly have I said that I am ready to preach the gospel to you Romans also: [[1:16|For I am not ashamed of the gospel|Non enim erubesco Evangelium]], that is, I am not abashed to proclaim publicly the cross and passion and the other mysteries of Christ which are described in the Gospel and are mocked by the reprobate. For I am ready to suffer reproach for the name of Jesus[[Acts 5:41||]], since He Himself says: [[Luke 9:26|he that shall be ashamed of me and of my words, of him the Son of man shall be ashamed|Qui me erubuerit et meos sermones, hunc Filius hominis erubescet]], when he shall come in his kingdom. With this agrees that word of the Psalmist: [[Ps 118:46|And I spoke of thy testimonies before kings: and I was not ashamed|Et loquebar in testimoniis tuis in conspectu regum, et non confundebar]]. The reason of this is added: [[1:16|For it is the power of God unto salvation to every one that believeth|Virtus enim Dei est in salutem omni credenti]], that is, the Gospel of Christ is power, that is, a mighty effect of the divine might, or a strong teaching, availing unto eternal salvation for every one who believes with a faith that is formed [that is, quickened by charity] and persevering; [[1:16|to the Jew first|Judæo primum]], that is, to those converted from Judaism, namely the primitive Church, which was made up of Jews. For Christ too said: [[Matt 15:24|I was not sent but to the sheep, that are lost of the house of Israel|Non sum missus nisi ad oves quæ perierunt domus Israel]], that is, I was sent first and principally to the Synagogue. Therefore Paul said to the Jews: [[Acts 13:46|To you it behoved us first to speak the word of God|Vobis oportebat primum loqui verbum Dei]]. Then [[1:16|and to the Greek|et Græco]], that is, to those converted from heathendom, the Gospel avails. By the Greeks, as by the worthier part, he signifies the Gentiles. For when the preaching of the Apostles was rejected by the Jews, a just passing over to the Gentiles took place, as Paul testifies: [[Acts 13:46|because you reject it and judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold we turn to the Gentiles|Quia repulistis illud, et indignos vos judicastis vitæ æternæ, ecce convertimur ad gentes]]. According to Haymo, the Gospel is called the power of God because it proclaims Christ the power of God[[1 Cor 1:24||]]. According to Ambrose, it is called the power of God because it avails for the forgiveness of sins and for the working of miracles.

paras.t: Quod autem Evangelium sit virtus Dei, proficiens in salutem omni credenti, consequenter declarat. Justitia enim Dei in eo revelatur ex fide in fidem. Hæc justitia Dei, quæ revelatur seu manifestatur in Evangelio, sicut in scriptura veraci, vel in Judæo et Græco, sicut in subjecto justificato, tripliciter intelligi potest : Primo, de increata justitia Creatoris, quæ est ipsemet Deus sanctus et justus. In Evangelio quippe increata Dei Patris justitia declaratur sive describitur : quomodo scilicet maluit Unigenitum suum pati et mori, quam peccata manere inulta; et quomodo Christus per viam justitiæ mundum redemit; quomodo etiam Pater omne judicium præstitit Christo, et per ipsum judicaturus est omnes, daturusque singulis quod merentur. Nunc tamen potissimum loquitur sanctus Apostolus de justitia Dei qua infideles et impii justificati sunt gratis. — Sed quum hoc ad misericordiam Dei pertineat, mirum videtur quomodo illud justitiæ adscribatur. Et respondendum, secundum Anselmum, quod tanta est bonitas atque benignitas Dei, ut justum sit eum etiam indignis et impiis misereri ac parcere. Sicque, ut hujusmodi actu attenditur justitia ex parte bonitatis divinæ secundum se ipsam acceptæ, misericordia quoque in eo attenditur ex parte bonitatis divinæ ad indignos relatæ. Secundo exponitur de justitia Dei creata, quam ipse causat in nobis : per quam justificamur formaliter, quia per eam Deus justificat nos gratis, per fidem sine operibus legis. Dando enim animæ fidem et gratiam, confert justitiam, per quam anima justificatur. Hæc justitia in Evangelio revelatur, et in Christianorum cordibus manifestatur. — Tertio exponitur de fideli ac vera divinarum promissionum adimpletione, qua Deus in Ecclesia et in Evangelio adimplevit quod in veteri Testamento prædixit, atque in populo Synagogæ præsignavit. Hæc justitia in Evangelio revelatur, Christo testante : Oportet impleri omnia quæ scripta sunt in lege et Prophetis et Psalmis de me; et alibi, Unum iota non peribit de lege, donec omnia fiant. De prædicta justitia Dei secundo modo accepta, alio loco dicit Apostolus, loquens de Judæis : Ignorantes Dei justitiam, et suam volentes statuere, justitiæ Dei non sunt subjecti ; et rursus, Inveniar in illo, non habens meam justitiam quæ ex lege est, sed quæ ex fide. Unde per Prophetam Dominus ait : Prope est justitia mea ut reveletur. Erat namque in veteri lege velata, sed in Evangelio est revelata. De qua justitia dicit Salvator : Qui crediderit et baptizatus fuerit, salvus erit ; et alibi, Fides tua te salvam fecit ; itemque, Qui credit in me, habet vitam æternam.
paras.en: That the Gospel is the power of God, availing unto salvation for every one who believes, he next shows: [[1:17|For the justice of God is revealed therein, from faith unto faith|Justitia enim Dei in eo revelatur ex fide in fidem]]. This justice of God, which is revealed or made manifest in the Gospel, as in a truthful writing, or in the Jew and the Greek, as in the subject justified, may be understood in three ways. First, of the uncreated justice of the Creator, which is God Himself, holy and just. For in the Gospel the uncreated justice of God the Father is declared or described: namely, how He chose that His Only-begotten should suffer and die rather than that sins should remain unpunished; and how Christ redeemed the world by the way of justice; how also the Father has given all judgment to Christ[[John 5:22||]], and through Him will judge all[[2 Tim 4:1||]], and give to each what he deserves. Yet here the holy Apostle speaks chiefly of the justice of God by which unbelievers and the ungodly are justified freely. — But since this belongs to the mercy of God, it seems strange how it is ascribed to justice. The answer, according to Anselm, is that so great is the goodness and kindness of God that it is just for Him to have mercy on and spare even the unworthy and the ungodly. And so, as justice is regarded in such an act on the side of the divine goodness taken in itself, mercy also is regarded in it on the side of the divine goodness as related to the unworthy. Secondly, it is expounded of the created justice of God, which He causes in us, by which we are formally justified, since by it God justifies us freely, through faith without the works of the law. For by giving the soul faith and grace He confers justice, by which the soul is justified. This justice is revealed in the Gospel and made manifest in the hearts of Christians. — Thirdly, it is expounded of the faithful and true fulfilment of the divine promises, by which God fulfilled in the Church and in the Gospel what He foretold in the Old Testament and prefigured in the people of the Synagogue. This justice is revealed in the Gospel, as Christ testifies: [[Luke 24:44|all things must needs be fulfilled which are written in the law of Moses and in the prophets and in the psalms, concerning me|Oportet impleri omnia quæ scripta sunt in lege et Prophetis et Psalmis de me]]; and elsewhere, [[Matt 5:18|one jot, or one tittle shall not pass of the law, till all be fulfilled|Unum iota non peribit de lege, donec omnia fiant]]. Of the aforesaid justice of God taken in the second way the Apostle says in another place, speaking of the Jews: [[Rom 10:3|not knowing the justice of God and seeking to establish their own, have not submitted themselves to the justice of God|Ignorantes Dei justitiam, et suam volentes statuere, justitiæ Dei non sunt subjecti]]; and again, [[Phil 3:9|may be found in him, not having my justice, which is of the law, but that which is of the faith|Inveniar in illo, non habens meam justitiam quæ ex lege est, sed quæ ex fide]]. Whence the Lord says by the Prophet: My justice is near, to be revealed [the margin gives Is. xlvi, 13; Denis's wording is closer to Is 56:1]. For it was veiled in the old law, but in the Gospel it is revealed. Of which justice the Saviour says: [[Mark 16:16|He that believeth and is baptized shall be saved|Qui crediderit et baptizatus fuerit, salvus erit]]; and elsewhere, [[Matt 9:22|thy faith hath made thee whole|Fides tua te salvam fecit]]; and again, [[John 6:47|He that believeth in me hath everlasting life|Qui credit in me, habet vitam æternam]].

paras.t: Quælibet justitia Dei nunc prædicta, revelatur ex fide in fidem, hoc est, ex fide Prophetarum et Patriarcharum, in fidem Apostolorum atque Ecclesiæ : quia quod illi crediderunt futurum, isti crediderunt impletum. Vel, Ex fide, id est ex actu fidei unius articuli, in fidem, hoc est in actum fidei alterius articuli. Omnia namque testimonia fidei sunt connexa, et unum ex alio magis credibile redditur, imo et quodammodo declaratur, magisque planum ac rationale judicatur. Sicut scriptum est : Justus autem ex fide vivit. Hoc allegat Apostolus ad probandum, quod justitia Dei revelatur in Evangelio, vel in Christiano, ex fide in fidem.
paras.en: Each justice of God just mentioned is revealed [[1:17|from faith unto faith|ex fide in fidem]], that is, from the faith of the Prophets and Patriarchs into the faith of the Apostles and of the Church: because what those believed as to come, these believed as fulfilled. Or, *from faith*, that is, from the act of faith in one article, *unto faith*, that is, into the act of faith in another article. For all the testimonies of the faith are linked together, and one is rendered more credible by another, nay, is in some manner made clear, and is judged more plain and reasonable. [[1:17|as it is written: The just man liveth by faith|Sicut scriptum est : Justus autem ex fide vivit]]. The Apostle adduces this to prove that the justice of God is revealed in the Gospel, or in the Christian, from faith unto faith.

paras.t: Sed quum fides sit una, juxta illud, Unus Dominus, una fides, unum baptisma : quomodo nunc dicitur, Ex fide in fidem, quasi sint fides diversæ ? Et respondendum, quod fides est una ex parte objecti. Numeratur autem et diversificatur ex parte subjectorum : in eodem tamen fides non est nisi una numero, sicut et caritas. Unde, ut dictum est, per fidem intelligitur actus fidei, qui diversificatur. — Auctoritas vero ab Apostolo introducta, habetur in Habacuc, ubi legitur : Ecce qui incredulus est, non erit recta anima ejus in semetipso ; justus autem in sua fide vivet. Cui concordat illud quoque Isaiæ : Qui incredulus est, infideliter agit. Unde in Ecclesiastico inducitur : Qui timetis Dominum, credite illi, et non evacuabitur merces vestra. Nullus etenim proprie justus est, nisi referat opera sua ad ultimum finem, qui est supernaturalis felicitas. Hunc autem finem non agnoscimus, nisi per fidem, quæ in omni actu meritorio dirigit rationem. Idcirco in fide, tanquam in basi seu fundamento virtutum, vivit justus. Hinc etiam ait Scriptura : Domine, oculi tui respiciunt fidem.
paras.en: But since faith is one, according to that word, [[Eph 4:5|One Lord, one faith, one baptism|Unus Dominus, una fides, unum baptisma]], how is it now said, *from faith unto faith*, as though there were different faiths? The answer is that faith is one on the side of its object; but it is numbered and diversified on the side of its subjects; yet in one and the same person faith is only one in number, as is charity also. Hence, as was said, by *faith* is understood the act of faith, which is diversified. — The authority brought in by the Apostle is found in Habacuc, where we read: [[Hab 2:4|Behold, he that is unbelieving, his soul shall not be right in himself: but the just shall live in his faith|Ecce qui incredulus est, non erit recta anima ejus in semetipso ; justus autem in sua fide vivet]]. With this agrees also that of Isaias: [[Is 21:2|he that is unfaithful dealeth unfaithfully|Qui incredulus est, infideliter agit]] [the printed margin reads Is. xxi, 2]. Hence it is said in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 2:8|Ye that fear the Lord, believe him: and your reward shall not be made void|Qui timetis Dominum, credite illi, et non evacuabitur merces vestra]]. For no one is properly just unless he refers his works to the last end, which is supernatural happiness. But this end we know only by faith, which directs reason in every meritorious act. Therefore the just man lives in faith, as in the base or foundation of the virtues. Hence too the Scripture says: [[Jer 5:3|O Lord, thy eyes are upon truth|Domine, oculi tui respiciunt fidem]] [the Vulgate has *fidem*, faith, which Denis follows; the Douay-Rheims renders it *truth*].

paras.t: Porro, quod ex fide sit salus justitiaque credentium, declarat consequenter Apostolus ex opposito. Revelatur enim ira Dei, id est justa ultio divinæ justitiæ, de cœlo, per revelationes cœlestes ab angelis factas, qui hominibus divinam districtionem ac ultionem, seu pœnas inferni, revelaverunt. Vel, Ira Dei de cœlo, id est Dei cœli, seu Dei cœlestis, de quo canitur, Laudate Dominum de cœlis ; vel, Dei judicis, de cœlo venturi ad judicandum vivos ac mortuos. Vel dicitur ira Dei revelari de cœlo, quia in die novissimo cœli ardentes (secundum Petrum apostolum), et angeli cum Judice venientes, ostendent iram Dei contra iniquos. Itaque revelatur ira, indignatio, detestatio Dei, super omnem impietatem, qua peccatur in Deum, et injustitiam, qua peccatur in proximum, hominum perversorum, eorum videlicet qui veritatem Dei quam agnoscunt, hoc est divinorum notitiam, seu divinam justitiam, quæ frequenter veritas nominatur, in injustitia detinent, id est, injuste vivendo apud se retinent, non procedentes in actum virtutis, sed ipsam veritatem ab operis executione retrahunt atque abscondunt : quibus competit illud, Scienti bonum et non facienti, peccatum est illi ; et illud, Melius erat non cognoscere viam justitiæ, quam post agnitionem retrorsum reverti. Hoc loco incipit loqui Apostolus contra peccata gentilium idololatrarum. De hac revelatione iræ Dei super impietatem et injustitiam hominum, ipse Dominus per Prophetam protestatur : Visitabo super orbis mala, et contra impios iniquitatem ipsorum ; et requiescere faciam superbiam infidelium, et arrogantiam fortium humiliabo.
paras.en: Further, that the salvation and justice of believers is from faith the Apostle next shows from the opposite: [[1:18|For the wrath of God|Revelatur enim ira Dei]] [[1:18|is revealed|Revelatur]], that is, the just vengeance of the divine justice, [[1:18|from heaven|de cælo]], through heavenly revelations made by the angels, who have revealed to men the divine severity and vengeance, or the pains of hell. Or, *the wrath of God from heaven*, that is, of the God of heaven, or the heavenly God, of whom it is sung, [[Ps 148:1|Praise ye the Lord from the heavens|Laudate Dominum de cœlis]]; or, of God the Judge, who will come from heaven to judge the living and the dead. Or the wrath of God is said to be revealed from heaven because on the last day the burning heavens (according to Peter the apostle)[[2 Pet 3:12||]], and the angels coming with the Judge[[Matt 16:27||]], will show forth the wrath of God against the wicked. So the wrath, indignation and abhorrence of God is revealed [[1:18|against all ungodliness|super omnem impietatem]], by which sin is committed against God, [[1:18|and injustice|et injustitiam]], by which sin is committed against one's neighbour, [[1:18|of those men|hominum eorum]], perverse men, namely of those [[1:18|that detain the truth of God|qui veritatem Dei]] which they know, that is, the knowledge of divine things, or the divine justice, which is often called truth, [[1:18|in injustice|in injustitia detinent]], that is, by living unjustly they keep it shut up within themselves, not going forward into the act of virtue, but withdrawing and hiding the truth itself from being carried out in deed. To them applies that word, [[Jas 4:17|who knoweth to do good and doth it not, to him it is sin|Scienti bonum et non facienti, peccatum est illi]]; and that, [[2 Pet 2:21|better for them not to have known the way of justice than, after they have known it, to turn back|Melius erat non cognoscere viam justitiæ, quam post agnitionem retrorsum reverti]]. Here the Apostle begins to speak against the sins of the idolatrous Gentiles. Of this revelation of the wrath of God against the ungodliness and injustice of men the Lord Himself protests by the Prophet: [[Is 13:11|And I will visit the evils of the world, and against the wicked for their iniquity: and I will make the pride of infidels to cease, and will bring down the arrogancy of the mighty.|Et visitabo super orbis mala, et contra impios iniquitatem eorum; et quiescere faciam superbiam infidelium, et arrogantiam fortium humiliabo.]].

paras.t: Insuper causa punitionis istorum subjungitur. Quia quod notum est Dei, hoc est, quod per naturalem rationem de Deo sciri potest, videlicet quod Deus sit justus et sapiens, approbans bona et reprobans mala, et quod ipsi soli sit cultus perfectissimus, utpote honor latriæ, exhibendus, manifestum est in illis, hoc est, gentilibus notum fuit. Deus enim illis revelavit per influentiam luminis naturalis, per quod anima rationalis ex creaturis intelligit Creatorem. De quo lumine scriptum est : Signatum est super nos lumen vultus tui, Domine. Unde Origenes ait : Notum Dei, est hoc quod ex mundi hujus dispositione et naturali ratione assequi possumus ; ignotum vero Dei, est ratio substantiæ ejus, quæ omnem latet creaturam, similiter et mysterium humanæ liberationis. Pluribus autem modis Deus revelavit hominibus veritatem, videlicet per sapientiæ infusionem, per angelicam revelationem, per Sanctorum instructionem, per naturalem rationem. Secundum Damascenum quoque, omnibus naturaliter inserta est cognitio exsistendi Deum. Nunc tamen agit Apostolus de revelatione quæ fit per naturalem rationem, quæ ex creaturis ascendit ad Creatoris notitiam.
paras.en: Moreover the cause of their punishment is added: [[1:19|Because that which is known of God|quia quod notum est Dei]], that is, what can be known of God by natural reason, namely that God is just and wise, approving good and condemning evil, and that to Him alone the most perfect worship, namely the honour of latria [the worship due to God alone], is to be shown, [[1:19|is manifest in them|manifestum est in illis]], that is, was known to the Gentiles. [[1:19|For God hath manifested it unto them|Deus enim illis manifestavit]] [Denis reads *revelavit*, revealed] through the inflowing of natural light, by which the rational soul understands the Creator from creatures. Of which light it is written: [[Ps 4:7|The light of thy countenance, O Lord, is signed upon us|Signatum est super nos lumen vultus tui, Domine]]. Whence Origen says: What is known of God is that which we can attain from the ordering of this world and by natural reason; but what is unknown of God is the nature of His substance, which is hidden from every creature, and likewise the mystery of man's deliverance. God has revealed the truth to men in several ways: by the infusion of wisdom, by angelic revelation, by the instruction of the Saints, and by natural reason. According to Damascene also, the knowledge that God exists is naturally implanted in all. Here, however, the Apostle treats of the revelation made through natural reason, which rises from creatures to the knowledge of the Creator.

paras.t: Subditur namque : Invisibilia enim ipsius, id est divina natura incorporea, simplex et invisibilis, et perfectiones ejus quæ naturaliter sciri possunt, videlicet justitia, potentia, providentia, etc., quæ dicuntur invisibilia Dei, quoniam licet sint unum in Deo et ipsa divina essentia, tamen secundum rationem distinguuntur, diversimode significantur, et per diversa cognoscuntur. Hæc ergo invisibilia Dei, a creatura mundi, id est ab homine, qui inter creaturas hujus sensibilis mundi primatum sortitur : de quo Dominus dicebat, Prædicate Evangelium omni creaturæ, id est omni homini ; per ea quæ facta sunt, id est per res creatas, intellecta, id est intellectualiter contemplata : oportet enim invisibilia Dei intellectuali puroque oculo intueri ; conspiciuntur, id est, agnoscuntur. Vel, Per ea quæ facta sunt intellecta, id est per creata rite considerata. Sempiterna quoque virtus ejus, id est æterna potestas Dei, et divinitas, ab homine conspiciuntur per ea quæ facta sunt, non utique per speciem, vel quid sint, sed quia sunt, et quid non sunt. Quum enim omnis creatura sit quidam radius sui creatoris, et omnis effectus sit quædam participata similitudo suæ causæ, quoniam unumquodque producit sibi simile : hinc certum est quod ex naturis creatis aliquo modo cognoscatur increata natura. Videntes quippe philosophi ordinem esse in rebus, et quod unum procedit, causatur et gubernatur ab alio, pervenerunt ad notitiam unius primi summique entis, quod oportuit esse æternum, perfectum et independens. Et uniformi quoque motu cælestium corporum, et stabili consistentia mundi atque gubernatione inferiorum a superioribus, perpenderunt esse in universo unum quemdam summum provisorem, dominatorem ac principem. Quam multa autem vera, profunda ac mira agnoverint Plato cum suis, et Aristoteles cum Peripateticis, de invisibilibus Dei, de sempiterna virtute ac divinitate ipsius, patet in libris eorum. Sed et Proclus Platonicus in Elementatione sua theologica, de Deo atque divinis subtilissime loquitur, quamvis in multis aberret. Prædictis autem verbis Apostoli consonat illud quoque Sapientis : A magnitudine speciei creaturæ poterit creator horum cognoscibiliter videri. Omnia enim, ut Salomon ait, propter se ipsum operatus est Dominus, scilicet ut in creaturis divina majestas atque perfectio refulgerent, sicque ex consideratione creaturarum incitaretur homo ad contemplationem, amorem, ac reverentiam Creatoris. Hinc scriptum est : Fecit Deus opera sua ut timeatur ; et iterum, Levate in excelsum oculos vestros, et videte quis creavit hæc.
paras.en: For it is added: [[1:20|For the invisible things of him|Invisibilia enim ipsius]], that is, the divine nature, incorporeal, simple and invisible, and His perfections that can be known naturally, namely justice, power, providence, etc., which are called the invisible things of God because, though in God they are one and the divine essence itself, yet they are distinguished in concept, are signified in different ways, and are known through different things. These invisible things of God, then, [[1:20|from the creation of the world|a creatura mundi]], that is, by man, who holds the first place among the creatures of this sensible world, of whom the Lord said, [[Mark 16:15|preach the gospel to every creature|Prædicate Evangelium omni creaturæ]], that is, to every man [Denis takes *a creatura mundi* as *by the creature of the world*]; [[1:20|by the things that are made|per ea quæ facta sunt]], that is, through created things, [[1:20|being understood|intellecta]], that is, contemplated intellectually, for the invisible things of God must be beheld with the pure eye of the intellect; [[1:20|are clearly seen|conspiciuntur]], that is, are known. Or, *understood by the things that are made*, that is, by created things duly considered. [[1:20|His eternal power also and divinity|sempiterna quoque ejus virtus, et divinitas]], that is, the eternal might of God, are seen by man through the things that are made, not indeed in their proper form, or what they are, but that they are, and what they are not. For since every creature is a kind of ray of its creator, and every effect is a certain participated likeness of its cause, since each thing produces its like, it is certain that from created natures the uncreated nature is in some way known. For the philosophers, seeing that there is order in things, and that one thing proceeds from, is caused and governed by another, came to the knowledge of one first and highest being, which must be eternal, perfect and independent. And from the uniform motion of the heavenly bodies, the stable consistency of the world, and the governance of lower things by higher, they judged that there is in the universe one supreme provider, ruler and prince. How many true, profound and wonderful things Plato with his followers, and Aristotle with the Peripatetics, knew of the invisible things of God, of His eternal power and divinity, is plain in their books. And Proclus the Platonist too, in his Elements of Theology, speaks most subtly of God and divine things, though he errs in many points. With these words of the Apostle agrees also that of the Wise Man: [[Wis 13:5|by the greatness of the beauty, and of the creature, the creator of them may be seen, so as to be known thereby|A magnitudine speciei creaturæ poterit creator horum cognoscibiliter videri]]. For, as Solomon says, [[Prov 16:4|The Lord hath made all things for himself|Omnia enim, ut Salomon ait, propter se ipsum operatus est Dominus]], namely that the divine majesty and perfection might shine forth in creatures, and so man might be stirred by the consideration of creatures to the contemplation, love and reverence of the Creator. Hence it is written: [[Eccles 3:14|God hath made that he may be feared|Fecit Deus opera sua ut timeatur]]; and again, [[Is 40:26|Lift up your eyes on high, and see who hath created these things|Levate in excelsum oculos vestros, et videte quis creavit hæc]].

paras.t: In tantum igitur cognoverunt Deum, ita ut sint inexcusabiles de suis peccatis, præsertim de idololatria. Non enim excusat eos ignorantia. Quia quum cognovissent Deum per naturalem rationem, secundum modum prætactum, non sicut Deum glorificaverunt, serviendo ei cum debita reverentia, aut gratias egerunt Deo pro beneficiis suis ; sed evanuerunt, hoc est, inanes effecti sunt, in cogitationibus suis vanis ac frivolis, glorificantes et magnipendentes se ipsos ; et obscuratum, luce gratiæ privatum, et splendore divinæ sapientiæ destitutum, est insipiens cor eorum, impletumque est caligine vitiorum, propter vanitatem cogitationum suarum. Unde scriptum est : Væ qui cogitatis inutile. Et alibi admonet Dominus : Auferte malum cogitationum vestrarum ab oculis meis. Per Salomonem quoque Sapientia Dei, Christus Dominus, contestatur : Ego, inquiens, Sapientia habito in consilio, et eruditis intersum cogitationibus.
paras.en: So far, then, did they know God, [[1:20|so that they are inexcusable|ita ut sint inexcusabiles]] for their sins, especially for idolatry; for ignorance does not excuse them. [[1:21|Because that, when they knew God|Quia cum cognovissent Deum]] by natural reason, in the manner touched on above, [[1:21|they have not glorified him as God|non sicut Deum glorificaverunt]], by serving Him with due reverence, [[1:21|or given thanks|aut gratias egerunt]] to God for His benefits; [[1:21|but became vain|sed evanuerunt]], that is, were made empty, [[1:21|in their thoughts|in cogitationibus suis]], vain and frivolous, glorifying and making much of themselves; [[1:21|was darkened|et obscuratum]], deprived of the light of grace and bereft of the splendour of divine wisdom, [[1:21|And their foolish heart|est insipiens cor eorum]], and was filled with the gloom of vices, because of the vanity of their thoughts. Whence it is written: [[Mich 2:1|Woe to you that devise that which is unprofitable|Væ qui cogitatis inutile]]. And elsewhere the Lord admonishes: [[Is 1:16|take away the evil of your devices from my eyes|Auferte malum cogitationum vestrarum ab oculis meis]]. By Solomon also the Wisdom of God, Christ the Lord, bears witness, saying: [[Prov 8:12|I, wisdom, dwell in counsel, and am present in learned thoughts|Ego … Sapientia habito … intersum cogitationibus]].

paras.t: Dicentes enim se esse sapientes, id est, se ipsos de sua sapientia jactantes, atque in se ipsis, non in fonte sapientiæ gloriantes, stulti facti sunt coram Deo seu divino judicio, qui stultam fecit sapientiam hujus mundi. Qui enim scientiam creaturarum et naturalem sapientiam divinorum non ordinat ad salutarem ac supernaturalem sapientiam, et Dei honorem, veraciter stultus est, tanquam contra ordinem rerum faciens, et contra censuram æternæ sapientiæ agens. Propter quod scriptum est : Stultus factus est omnis homo a scientia sua ; et iterum, Sapientia tua et scientia tua decepit te ; et rursus, Væ qui sapientes estis in oculis vestris. — Sed videntur hæc de philosophis verificari non posse. Quum enim quidam interrogasset Pythagoram, an sapiens esset, dixit se sapientem non esse, sed philosophum, id est sapientiæ amatorem. Et ejus exemplo posteri ejus se non vocaverunt sapientes, sed philosophos. Et respondendum, quod licet non dicerent ore, corde tamen dicebant se sapientes, paucissimis forsan exceptis, qui nec idola coluerunt : de quibus modo non agitur.
paras.en: [[1:22|For, professing themselves to be wise|Dicentes enim se esse sapientes]], that is, boasting of their own wisdom and glorying in themselves, not in the fountain of wisdom, [[1:22|they became fools|stulti facti sunt]] before God or in the divine judgement, who has [[1 Cor 1:20|made foolish the wisdom of this world?|stultam fecit sapientiam hujus mundi]]. For he who does not order the knowledge of creatures and the natural wisdom of divine things to saving and supernatural wisdom and to the honour of God is truly a fool, as acting against the order of things and against the verdict of the eternal wisdom. Therefore it is written: [[Jer 51:17|Every man is become foolish by his knowledge|Stultus factus est omnis homo a scientia sua]]; and again, [[Is 47:10|Thy wisdom, and, thy knowledge, this hath deceived thee|Sapientia tua et scientia tua decepit te]]; and once more, [[Is 5:21|Woe to you that are wise in your own eyes|Væ qui sapientes estis in oculis vestris]]. — But it seems this cannot be verified of the philosophers. For when someone asked Pythagoras whether he was wise, he said he was not wise but a philosopher, that is, a lover of wisdom; and following his example his successors called themselves not wise men but philosophers. The answer is that though they did not say it with their mouth, yet in their heart they said they were wise, except perhaps a very few who did not worship idols, of whom there is no question here.

paras.t: Et mutaverunt gloriam incorruptibilis Dei, in similitudinem imaginis corruptibilis hominis, id est, cultum, honorem et gloriam immortali et invariabili Deo impendendam, exhibuerunt imaginibus, statuis seu idolis hominum mortuorum, et volucrum, et quadrupedum, et serpentium. Quam verum sit hoc, in libro Sapientiæ prolixe describitur. Quomodo etiam populus Judæorum tanto errori subjacuit, talpasque ac vespertiliones adoravit, Isaias atque Ezechiel prosequuntur. Quidam autem gentilium ipsas imagines, quidam vero res significatas per imagines coluerunt.
paras.en: [[1:23|And they changed the glory of the incorruptible God into the likeness of the image of a corruptible man|Et mutaverunt gloriam incorruptibilis Dei, in similitudinem imaginis corruptibilis hominis]], that is, the worship, honour and glory to be paid to the immortal and unchangeable God they showed to images, statues or idols of dead men, [[1:23|and of birds, and of fourfooted beasts and of creeping things|et volucrum, et quadrupedum, et serpentium]]. How true this is is described at length in the book of Wisdom[[Wis 13:1||]] [the margin gives Wis. xiii–xv]. How the people of the Jews also fell into so great an error and worshipped moles and bats, Isaias and Ezechiel relate[[Is 2:20||]][[Ezech 8:10||]]. Some of the Gentiles worshipped the images themselves, others the things signified by the images.

paras.t: Propter quod, id est propter idololatriam jam prædictam, quæ omnis peccati origo efficitur, juxta illud Sapientis : Infandorum idolorum cultura, omnis mali causa est, et principium et finis ; tradidit illos Deus, non effective, sed permissive, gratiam suam justissime subtrahendo, in desideria cordis eorum, id est in inordinatos appetitus et concupiscentias carnis, videlicet, in immunditiam luxuriæ, vel potius Sodomiticæ maculæ; ut contumeliis, hoc est actibus ipsi naturæ injuriosis, nocivis atque contrariis, afficiant corpora sua in semetipsis, hoc est, in eodem sexu atque supposito, committendo peccata contra naturam. Vel, in semetipsis, id est ad invicem : nam et qui fornicatur, peccat in corpus suum.
paras.en: [[1:24|Wherefore|Propter quod]], that is, because of the idolatry already mentioned, which becomes the origin of every sin, according to the word of the Wise Man: [[Wis 14:27|the worship of abominable idols is the cause, and the beginning and end of all evil|Infandorum idolorum cultura, omnis mali causa est, et principium et finis]]; [[1:24|God gave them up|tradidit illos Deus]], not by causing it but by permitting it, most justly withdrawing His grace, [[1:24|to the desires of their heart|in desideria cordis eorum]], that is, to disordered appetites and lusts of the flesh, namely [[1:24|unto uncleanness|in immunditiam]] of lechery, or rather of the Sodomitic stain; [[1:24|to dishonour|ut contumeliis]], that is, by acts injurious, harmful and contrary to nature itself, [[1:24|their own bodies among themselves|afficiant corpora sua in semetipsis]], that is, within the same sex and person [*suppositum*], committing sins against nature. Or, *among themselves*, that is, with one another: for [[1 Cor 6:18|he that committeth fornication sinneth against his own body|qui fornicatur, peccat in corpus suum]].

paras.t: Qui commutaverunt veritatem Dei in mendacium, id est, divinitatem, honorem et gloriam, soli vero omnipotentique Deo adscribenda et exhibenda, transtulerunt ad deos falsos seu idola, et coluerunt et servierunt creaturæ, videlicet idolis suis, potius quam Creatori, qui est Deus benedictus in sæcula, amen. Ecce quanta perversitas. Hæc traditio impiorum in desideria cordis eorum, est gravissima pœna quam Deus in præsenti infligit. Et est pœna damni, cui in inferno correspondet carentia beatificæ fruitionis. Unde Dominus ait in Psalmo : Dimisi eos secundum desideria cordis eorum ; ibunt in adinventionibus suis. Unum namque peccatum trahit ad aliud, idemque peccatum est peccatum et causa peccati, seu culpa et pœna culpæ. Nam homo unum committendo peccatum, meretur a Deo relinqui, atque in aliud prolabi. Et quanto aliquis se ipsum erigit altius, inaniusque extollit, tanto meretur profundius cadere. Maxime quoque, qui tam sapientes sunt in propriis oculis, merentur relinqui, in tantum ut vitia carnis incidant, quæ sunt præcipue bestialia atque turpissima. Unde jam subditur :
paras.en: [[1:25|Who changed the truth of God into a lie|Qui commutaverunt veritatem Dei in mendacium]], that is, the divinity, honour and glory to be ascribed and shown to the one true and almighty God alone they transferred to false gods or idols, [[1:25|and worshipped and served the creature|et coluerunt, et servierunt creaturæ]], namely their idols, [[1:25|rather than the Creator, who is blessed for ever. Amen|potius quam Creatori, qui est Deus benedictus in sæcula, amen]] [Denis reads: who is God blessed for ever]. Behold how great a perversity! This giving up of the ungodly to the desires of their heart is the heaviest punishment that God inflicts in this present life. And it is a pain of loss [*pœna damni*, the punishment of being deprived of good], to which in hell there corresponds the want of the beatific enjoyment. Whence the Lord says in the Psalm: [[Ps 80:13|So I let them go according to the desires of their heart: they shall walk in their own inventions|Dimisi eos secundum desideria cordis eorum ; ibunt in adinventionibus suis]]. For one sin draws to another, and the same sin is both sin and the cause of sin, or guilt and the punishment of guilt. For by committing one sin a man deserves to be forsaken by God and to slip into another. And the higher a man raises himself and the more emptily he exalts himself, the deeper he deserves to fall. Above all, those who are so wise in their own eyes[[Is 5:21||]] deserve to be forsaken, so far as to fall into the vices of the flesh, which are especially bestial and most foul. Hence it is now added:

paras.t: Propterea tradidit illos Deus in passiones ignominiæ, id est in innominabilia vitia carnis, quæ sunt peccata contra naturam. Ignominia enim dicitur, quasi sine nomine dignitatis, quoniam talia scelera non faciliter explicantur. Prosequitur tamen Apostolus species tanti facinoris. Nam feminæ eorum immutaverunt naturalem usum, in eum usum qui est contra naturam, hoc est, organo sui sexus, quod ordinatur ad conceptionem prolis, abusæ sunt, ita ut femina feminæ misceretur. Similiter autem et masculi, relicto naturali usu feminæ, id est legitima seu naturali commixtione ac copula cum muliere, exarserunt igne libidinis in desideriis suis turpissimis in invicem, scilicet, masculi in masculos turpitudinem operantes, polluendo se mutuo variis modis. Sed et si masculus feminæ commisceatur alio modo, loco, seu organo, quam natura concessit, contra naturam peccatur. Et mercedem, quam oportuit, erroris sui in semetipsis recipientes. Sic construenda et intelligenda est littera : Prædicti idololatræ ac Sodomitici, recipientes a Deo permissive, a se ipsis autem causaliter : recipientes, inquam, et sustinentes in semetipsis, id est in propria natura, mercedem sui erroris, id est retributionem seu præmium suæ idololatriæ, scilicet traditionem et lapsum in passiones ignominiæ : quam mercedem oportuit vel decuit eos recipere secundum dictamen ac ordinem divinæ justitiæ, qua vitia vitiis proportionaliter puniuntur. Unde quemadmodum jactantia propriæ sapientiæ meruit ut in idololatriam caderent, sic idololatria, propter gravissimam suam deformitatem, meruit ut innominabilia carnis peccata inciderent.
paras.en: [[1:26|For this cause, God delivered them up to shameful affections|Propterea tradidit illos Deus in passiones ignominiæ]], that is, to the unnameable vices of the flesh, which are sins against nature. For *ignominia* is so called as being without the name of dignity [*in-* + *nomen*], since such crimes are not easily spoken of. Yet the Apostle sets out the kinds of so great a crime. [[1:26|For their women have changed the natural use into that use which is against nature|Nam feminæ eorum immutaverunt naturalem usum, in eum usum qui est contra naturam]], that is, they abused the organ of their sex, which is ordered to the conception of offspring, so that woman was joined with woman. [[1:27|And, in like manner, the men also, leaving the natural use of the women|Similiter autem et masculi, relicto naturali usu feminæ]], that is, lawful or natural intercourse and union with a woman, [[1:27|have burned in their lusts, one towards another|exarserunt in desideriis suis in invicem]] with the fire of lust in their most shameful desires, namely, [[1:27|men with men, working that which is filthy|masculi in masculos turpitudinem operantes]], defiling one another in various ways. And even if a man is joined with a woman in another manner, place or organ than nature has granted, sin is committed against nature. [[1:27|and receiving in themselves the recompense which was due to their error|Et mercedem, quam oportuit, erroris sui in semetipsis recipientes]]. The text is to be construed and understood thus: The aforesaid idolaters and Sodomites, *receiving*, from God by permission, but from themselves as cause; receiving, I say, and undergoing *in themselves*, that is, in their own nature, *the recompense of their error*, that is, the requital or reward of their idolatry, namely being given up and falling into shameful affections: *which* recompense *was due*, or was fitting for them to receive according to the dictate and order of the divine justice, by which vices are punished by vices in due proportion. Hence, just as the boasting of their own wisdom deserved that they should fall into idolatry, so idolatry, because of its most grievous deformity, deserved that they should fall into the unnameable sins of the flesh.

paras.t: Et sicut non probaverunt, hoc est, non putaverunt nec opere ostenderunt, Deum habere in notitia actus humanos, id est, æstimaverunt Deum non cognoscere peccata hominum, dicentes illud Job : Deus excelsior cœlo est, nec nostra considerat, et circa cardines cœli perambulat; et illud Ezechielis, Dereliquit Dominus terram, et Dominus nos non videt; tradidit illos Deus in reprobum sensum, hoc est in intellectum perversum, privando eos lumine gratiæ ac veræ sapientiæ, quatenus, sicut circa divinum intellectum erraverunt, sic in suo intellectu punirentur. Tales sunt omnes qui divinam providentiam negant. De quibus ait Psalmista : Dixerunt, Non videbit Dominus, nec intelliget Deus Jacob; et Sophonias, Dicunt, Non faciet Dominus bene, et non faciet male. Contra quos Dominus loquitur per Amos prophetam : Cognovi multa scelera vestra, et fortia peccata vestra. Vel sic : Sicut non probaverunt, hoc est, non curaverunt, Deum habere in notitia, id est cognoscere Deum veraciter, tradidit illos in reprobum sensum, excæcando corda ipsorum permissive, ita quod eis convenit illud propheticum : Sapientes sunt ut faciant mala, bene autem facere nescierunt. Ut faciant ea quæ non conveniunt, hoc est, quæ Deo, rationi, atque Ecclesiæ contrariantur. Hæc dictio, Ut, non tenetur hoc loco causaliter, sed concomitanter. Non enim idcirco tradidit illos in reprobum sensum directe, ut faciant mala; sed operatio mali consecuta est traditionem, seu derelictionem ipsorum prædictam. Sicque frequenter in libro isto accipitur.
paras.en: [[1:28|And as they liked not|Et sicut non probaverunt]], that is, did not think nor show by their deeds, [[1:28|to have God in their knowledge|Deum habere in notitia]] human acts [Denis reads: that God has human acts in His knowledge], that is, they reckoned that God does not know the sins of men, saying that word of Job: [[Job 22:12|God is higher than heaven|Deus excelsior cœlo est]], [[Job 22:14|he doth not consider our things, and he walketh about the poles of heaven|nec nostra considerat, et circa cardines cœli perambulat]]; and that of Ezechiel, [[Ezech 9:9|The Lord hath forsaken the earth, and the Lord seeth not|Dereliquit Dominus terram, et Dominus nos non videt]]; [[1:28|God delivered them up to a reprobate sense|tradidit illos Deus in reprobum sensum]], that is, to a perverse understanding, depriving them of the light of grace and of true wisdom, so that as they erred about the divine understanding, they should be punished in their own understanding. Such are all who deny the divine providence. Of whom the Psalmist says: [[Ps 93:7|And they have said: The Lord shall not see: neither shall the God of Jacob understand|Dixerunt, Non videbit Dominus, nec intelliget Deus Jacob]]; and Sophonias, They say, [[Soph 1:12|The Lord will not do good, nor will he do evil|Non faciet Dominus bene, et non faciet male]]. Against whom the Lord speaks by the prophet Amos: [[Amos 5:12|I know your manifold crimes, and your grievous sins|Cognovi multa scelera vestra, et fortia peccata vestra]]. Or thus: *As they liked not*, that is, cared not, *to have God in their knowledge*, that is, to know God truly, He delivered them up to a reprobate sense, blinding their hearts by permission, so that that prophetic word fits them: [[Jer 4:22|they are wise to do evil, but to do good they have no knowledge|Sapientes sunt ut faciant mala, bene autem facere nescierunt]]. [[1:28|to do those things which are not convenient|ut faciant ea quæ non conveniunt]], that is, things contrary to God, to reason and to the Church. The word *ut* [*to*, *so that*] is not taken here causally but concomitantly. For He did not directly deliver them to a reprobate sense in order that they might do evil; but the doing of evil followed upon their being given up, or forsaken, as said. And so it is often taken in this book.

paras.t: Sic ergo tradidit illos Deus repletos omni iniquitate, hoc est omni peccato. Peccatum enim iniquitas est, id est contra justitiam, secundum Joannem. Præterea, ponit partes seu species iniquitatis : malitia, qua alter alteri damnum inferre conatur; fornicatione, hoc est illegitimo cum muliere concubitu; avaritia, hoc est inordinato appetitu temporalium rerum, nequitia, id est perversitate, seu temeritate nefaria, plenos invidia, quæ est tristitia de bono alterius; homicidiis, contentione, dolo; malignitate, hoc est voluntate igne malitiæ inflammata; susurrones, hoc est discordiæ seminatores : contra quos Moyses præcipit, Non eris susurro in populo; et Ecclesiasticus ait : Susurro et bilinguis maledictus; multos enim turbavit pacem habentes. Detractores, hoc est aliorum famam denigrantes, de eorum defectibus inordinate loquendo, vel falsa imponendo. Deo odibiles quantum ad culpam. Odio enim Deo sunt impius, et impietas ejus. Unde Ecclesiastes ait : Si mordeat serpens in silentio, nihil minus eo habet qui occulte detrahit. Agendum est ergo quod ait vir sanctus : Detrahentem secreto proximo suo, hunc persequebar. Contumeliosos, id est verbis vel actibus injuriantes. Quod valde iniquum est, juxta illud : Homo assuetus in verbis improperii, omnibus diebus vitæ suæ non dirigetur. Superbos, appetendo honores; elatos, nolendo habere æqualem aut superiorem; inventores malorum, excogitando novos errores, aut culpas; parentibus non obedientes; insipientes, male sentiendo de rebus divinis; incompositos moribus, sine affectione, id est tepidos, carentes zelo justitiæ et caritatis fervore, absque fœdere, id est observatione pacti, societatis et amicitiæ. Unde scriptum est : Qui dissolvit pactum, numquid effugiet? Sine misericordia, id est crudeles. Viscera namque impiorum crudelia. In talibus adimpletur quod Jacobus ait : Judicium sine misericordia fiet ei qui non fecerit misericordiam.
paras.en: So then God delivered them up, [[1:29|Being filled with all iniquity|repletos omni iniquitate]], that is, with every sin. For [[1 John 3:4|sin is iniquity|Peccatum enim iniquitas est]], that is, against justice, according to John. Further, he sets down the parts or kinds of iniquity: [[1:29|malice|malitia]], by which one tries to do another harm; [[1:29|fornication|fornicatione]], that is, unlawful lying with a woman; [[1:29|avarice|avaritia]], that is, disordered craving for temporal things; [[1:29|wickedness|nequitia]], that is, perversity, or wicked rashness; [[1:29|full of envy|plenos invidia]], which is sorrow at another's good; [[1:29|murder, contention, deceit|homicidio, contentione, dolo]]; [[1:29|malignity|malignitate]], that is, a will inflamed with the fire of malice; [[1:29|whisperers|susurrones]], that is, sowers of discord: against whom Moses commands, [[Lev 19:16|Thou shalt not be a detractor nor a whisperer among the people|Non eris susurro in populo]]; and Ecclesiasticus says: [[Ecclus 28:15|The whisperer and the double tongue is accursed: for he hath troubled many that were at peace|Susurro et bilinguis maledictus; multos enim turbavit pacem habentes]]. [[1:30|Detractors|Detractores]], that is, blackening the good name of others by speaking inordinately of their faults or by imputing falsehoods. [[1:30|hateful to God|Deo odibiles]] as regards guilt. For [[Wis 14:9|to God the wicked and his wickedness are hateful alike|Odio enim Deo sunt impius, et impietas ejus]]. Whence Ecclesiastes says: [[Eccles 10:11|If a serpent bite in silence, he is nothing better that backbiteth secretly|Si mordeat serpens in silentio, nihil minus eo habet qui occulte detrahit]]. We must do, then, what the holy man says: [[Ps 100:5|The man that in private detracted his neighbour, him did I persecute|Detrahentem secreto proximo suo, hunc persequebar]]. [[1:30|contumelious|contumeliosos]], that is, wronging others by words or deeds; which is very wicked, according to that word: [[Ecclus 23:20|The man that is accustomed to opprobrious words, will never be corrected all the days of his life|Homo assuetus in verbis improperii, omnibus diebus vitæ suæ non dirigetur]]. [[1:30|proud|superbos]], by seeking honours; [[1:30|haughty|elatos]], by being unwilling to have an equal or a superior; [[1:30|inventors of evil things|inventores malorum]], by devising new errors or faults; [[1:30|disobedient to parents|parentibus non obedientes]]; [[1:31|Foolish|insipientes]], by thinking wrongly of divine things; [[1:31|dissolute|incompositos]] in their manners; [[1:31|without affection|sine affectione]], that is, lukewarm, lacking zeal for justice and the fervour of charity; [[1:31|without fidelity|absque fœdere]], that is, without keeping of covenant, fellowship and friendship. Whence it is written: [[Ezech 17:15|shall he that hath done thus prosper, or be saved? and shall he escape that hath broken the covenant?|Qui dissolvit pactum, numquid effugiet]]? [[1:31|without mercy|sine misericordia]], that is, cruel. For [[Prov 12:10|the bowels of the wicked are cruel|Viscera namque impiorum crudelia]]. In such is fulfilled what James says: [[Jas 2:13|judgment without mercy to him that hath not done mercy|Judicium sine misericordia fiet ei qui non fecerit misericordiam]].

paras.t: Qui quum justitiam Dei, hoc est justum Deum, cognovissent, non tamen intellexerunt, hoc scilicet, quoniam qui talia agunt, digni sunt morte æterna; et non solum qui ea faciunt sunt digni morte, sed etiam qui consentiunt facientibus, ut nullus excusetur.
paras.en: [[1:32|Who, having known the justice of God|Qui cum justitiam Dei cognovissent]], that is, the just God, [[1:32|did not understand|non intellexerunt]] this, namely, [[1:32|that they who do such things, are worthy of death|quoniam qui talia agunt, digni sunt morte]] eternal; [[1:32|and not only they that do them|et non solum qui ea faciunt]] are worthy of death, [[1:32|but they also that consent to them that do them|sed etiam qui consentiunt facientibus]], so that none may be excused.
